summary:
LOST SIGNAL: 10 DAYS is a browser-based 2D pixel-art educational game designed for children aged 7–12. Players become astronauts at ARES-7, a fictional Mars research outpost damaged by a powerful dust storm. With the help of NOVA, a robot companion, they must complete a ten-day mission to repair the base, protect the crew, conduct scientific research and restore communication with Earth.
The game combines five interconnected systems: life support, power management, radiation protection, food production and communication. Through five interactive mini-games and mission-based challenges, players repair oxygen systems, restore electrical circuits, grow plants, explore Mars and analyze rock samples. Their decisions affect resources and mission outcomes, teaching them to balance competing priorities.
NASA scientific resources and mission findings inform the game's educational content and selected mechanics, while in-game readings and scenarios are simulated.
By turning complex space engineering concepts into hands-on challenges, LOST SIGNAL makes STEM learning more engaging and helps young players develop critical thinking, problem-solving and systems-thinking skills.
details:
LOST SIGNAL: 10 DAYS

A Mars Survival, Science & Engineering Adventure

1. Detailed Project Description

LOST SIGNAL: 10 DAYS is a browser-based, interactive 2D pixel-art educational game designed for children aged 7–12. It transforms the challenges of a Mars research mission into a hands-on learning experience where players must understand, repair and manage interconnected spacecraft and habitat systems to keep an astronaut crew alive.

The game takes place at ARES-7, a fictional scientific research outpost on Mars. Following a powerful dust storm, several base systems are damaged and communication with Earth is lost. The astronaut wakes up inside the outpost and discovers that the station requires immediate repairs. With the help of NOVA, a robot companion, the player must complete a ten-day mission, restore essential systems, conduct scientific research and eventually re-establish communication with Earth.

Rather than presenting space science through passive explanations, LOST SIGNAL allows players to experience engineering decisions directly. Every action has consequences: energy spent on one system may become unavailable for another, water-saving strategies can affect the research environment, and neglecting life-support systems can threaten the crew.

The project combines storytelling, exploration, engineering challenges, resource management and simplified scientific simulations to make complex STEM concepts understandable and engaging for younger audiences.

2. How It Works — The 10-Day Mission

The experience is structured as a ten-day mission, with each day introducing a new challenge, scientific concept or engineering responsibility. Tasks gradually become more complex as players gain access to additional rooms, equipment and exploration opportunities.

DAY 1 — LOST SIGNAL

The astronaut wakes up in the damaged ARES-7 outpost. Players inspect the central computer, check energy reserves, communicate with NOVA, repair an oxygen leak and fix three damaged electrical cables. The first day introduces the base environment, inspection procedures and the importance of maintaining essential systems.

DAY 2 — SYSTEM CHECK

Players perform a detailed inspection of life-support equipment and restore emergency power distribution. An interactive electrical routing challenge requires them to connect available energy to critical systems. System checks introduce concepts such as atmospheric composition, ventilation, battery reserves and the differences between Earth's and Mars' environments.

DAY 3 — POWER DOWN

The player repairs a damaged electrical circuit through the Power Circuit mini-game and activates greenhouse lighting. This mission demonstrates how electrical connections support other habitat systems and how energy availability affects food production.

DAY 4 — DUST ON THE HORIZON

The first surface expedition begins. Before leaving the base, players must prepare a spacesuit, oxygen supply, battery, radio and scanner. Outside, they clean and align solar panels, explore the Martian environment and collect scientific samples. The mission introduces solar energy, dust accumulation, spacesuit oxygen management and Mars' lower gravity.

DAY 5 — THE LONG STORM

A major dust storm blocks sunlight and prevents surface exploration. Players must decide how to distribute limited energy between life support, greenhouse heating and scientific sample preservation. The storm demonstrates why mission planning and prioritization are essential when renewable energy becomes temporarily unavailable.

DAY 6 — WATER UNDER PRESSURE

Players conduct a greenhouse experiment, adjust conditions for healthy plant growth and choose between different water-supply strategies. They can invest energy in water recycling or extract water from a simulated underground frost location, which carries an environmental cost within the game. A scout drone exploration task introduces remote surface observation.

DAY 7 — RADIATION WARNING

A simulated solar radiation event creates an emergency. Players must transport water containers into a radiation shelter, activate its protective shield and take cover. The challenge demonstrates how shielding materials can reduce radiation exposure and why astronauts need to monitor space-weather conditions.

DAY 8 — READING THE ROCKS

Players analyze three collected Martian samples using the Rock Analyzer. They investigate mineral characteristics, connect findings to geological processes and place a research beacon at Rock Arch. The mission introduces planetary geology, mineral identification and the scientific importance of careful sample collection.

DAY 9 — THE FINAL REPAIR

Players restore power to the communication room, repair the antenna and complete the Antenna Signal mini-game. They can also prepare a scientific report containing research results, weather observations, drone surveys and greenhouse experiments. The mission introduces the enormous distances involved in communicating between Earth and Mars.

DAY 10 — HOME SIGNAL

The final mission requires players to allocate 40 units of energy to the main transmitter and send a signal back to Earth. After completing the transmission, players receive a mission outcome based on their decisions, collected samples, research progress and crew condition.

The ten-day structure creates a progression from basic inspection and repairs to independent exploration, scientific investigation and mission completion.

3. Core Engineering Systems

The game is built around five interconnected systems. They are not isolated activities: decisions affecting one system can influence several others.

3.1 Life Support

Life support represents the systems necessary to maintain a habitable environment. Players monitor oxygen, water and crew health, repair leaks and manage limited supplies.

Oxygen availability depends on maintaining the relevant equipment and supplying energy to essential systems. During surface exploration, the astronaut also consumes oxygen from the spacesuit. If the suit supply runs out, the astronaut returns to the base and the game applies a penalty to the base oxygen reserve.

The system teaches players that breathable air and reliable life support are essential requirements for human space exploration.

3.2 Power Management

Energy is a shared resource used throughout the outpost. Players repair electrical circuits, manage batteries, activate equipment and decide which systems receive power.

Solar generation is affected by environmental conditions. During the dust storm, sunlight becomes unavailable, forcing players to prioritize essential systems.

For example, powering greenhouse heaters can protect food production but leaves less energy for optional laboratory equipment. The player must balance immediate survival needs against longer-term research goals.

3.3 Radiation Protection

The radiation system introduces one of the major hazards of human exploration beyond Earth.

Players monitor simplified radiation readings, respond to a simulated solar event and prepare a shelter using water containers and an active shield.

The game demonstrates the principle of shielding through material mass and the importance of planning protective infrastructure before an emergency occurs.

3.4 Food Production

The greenhouse system demonstrates how controlled environments can support future space missions.

Players manage water, light, temperature and growing conditions through interactive experiments. Plant health depends on maintaining suitable environmental conditions and providing sufficient energy.

The greenhouse also creates a connection between power management and food availability: lighting and heating require energy, while neglecting environmental conditions can reduce food supplies.

3.5 Communication

Communication is essential for sending scientific information and restoring contact with Earth.

Players repair the antenna, activate the transmitter and prepare a scientific report. The game introduces communication delays caused by the distance between Earth and Mars.

For one scenario, the game uses a simplified Earth–Mars distance of approximately 225 million kilometers and calculates a one-way light-travel time of approximately 12 minutes and 31 seconds. This is an illustrative distance scenario, not a live measurement.

Together, these five systems introduce systems thinking: players learn that a successful space mission depends on the interaction of multiple technologies rather than one individual piece of equipment.

4. Gameplay Mechanics and Interactive Challenges

LOST SIGNAL contains five principal mini-games, each designed around a simplified engineering or scientific task.

1. Power Circuit

Players rotate electrical components to create a complete connection between a battery and powered equipment. The challenge introduces electrical circuits, energy distribution and troubleshooting.

2. Oxygen System Repair

Players identify air leaks, connect the correct pipes and maintain pressure within a safe operating range. It introduces basic concepts of pneumatic systems, pressure and life support.

3. Solar Panel Alignment

Players remove accumulated dust, adjust panel orientation and monitor the energy output. The activity introduces solar energy and the effect of environmental conditions on power generation.

4. Greenhouse Challenge

Players adjust water, lighting, temperature and growing time to maintain healthy plant conditions. The challenge introduces controlled-environment agriculture and experimental thinking.

5. Antenna Signal

Players tune a communication dial and maintain a stable signal despite interference. It introduces signal transmission, communication equipment and the challenges of deep-space communication.

In addition to these mini-games, the project includes an emergency power-distribution challenge, system-inspection quizzes, surface exploration, sample collection, drone operation, resource-management decisions and equipment upgrades.

Challenges include instructions, NOVA hints, explanations and opportunities to retry. This allows younger players to learn through experimentation rather than being discouraged by failure.

5. NOVA — The Robotic Mission Companion

NOVA is the astronaut's robotic companion and an important part of the learning experience.

Rather than functioning only as a decorative character, NOVA guides players through the mission and helps them understand unfamiliar systems.

NOVA provides daily briefings, explains scientific concepts, offers contextual hints, reacts to player actions and guides the astronaut toward important objectives. The robot also contributes to the Engineering Journal, recording mission activities and helping players follow their progress.

NOVA uses scripted dialogue and predefined game logic; it is not a live AI chatbot or an independently learning machine-learning system.

This approach provides a consistent and age-appropriate guide while keeping the experience accessible to younger players.

6. NASA Science and Research Integration

Scientific accuracy is an important part of LOST SIGNAL. NASA research, mission findings and publicly available scientific resources inform selected environmental parameters, educational explanations and gameplay concepts.

The project draws on several areas of space exploration:

  • Mars environmental conditions: NASA's Mars Fact Sheet informs educational content about the planet's atmosphere, gravity and physical environment.
  • MEDA (Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer): Research from the Perseverance rover's weather instrument informs the game's simulated weather conditions, including temperature, wind and dust-related concepts.
  • Curiosity RAD (Radiation Assessment Detector): Radiation measurements from the Curiosity mission inform the scientific basis of the radiation system. The outdoor reference rate used in the game is approximately 0.64 mSv per day, based on published Curiosity RAD findings.
  • PIXL and SHERLOC: Perseverance's scientific instruments inspire the game's rock-analysis activities and explanations of how researchers investigate Martian materials.
  • Ingenuity Mars Helicopter: The Ingenuity mission inspires the concept of using a small aerial vehicle for remote surface exploration. The in-game drone is a simplified fictional implementation, not a replica of Ingenuity's specifications.
  • ISS technologies: NASA's Veggie and Advanced Plant Habitat research inform the greenhouse concept. International Space Station life-support and water-recovery technologies provide scientific context for resource recycling.
  • Deep Space Network: NASA's deep-space communication infrastructure informs the game's communication theme and simplified signal-delay calculations.

Scientific Data and Simulation Disclaimer

NASA resources are used as scientific references to inform selected game mechanics, parameters and educational content. The game does not download NASA datasets or connect to live NASA APIs.

In-game readings, environmental scenarios and certain system values are simulated or simplified for educational gameplay. ARES-7, its astronaut, NOVA, the mission storyline and its specific events are fictional. The project does not claim to reproduce an actual NASA mission or operational spacecraft system.

7. Testing, Mission Outcomes and Educational Impact

Testing focused on the functionality of the ten-day mission, interactions between the core systems, mini-game behavior and the ability to complete a full playthrough.

Playwright was used for automated browser testing. An automated ten-day playthrough successfully reached the Successful Mission ending without encountering gameplay errors.

The game includes multiple possible outcomes:

  • Successful Mission: The player completes the research objectives, analyzes at least three rock samples, reaches the required research progress and maintains sufficient crew health.
  • Survival First: The player completes the mission but does not meet all the conditions for the full research outcome.
  • Damaged Research Sites: The player makes decisions that reduce environmental and research-site protection below the required threshold.
  • Mission Failed: Crew health reaches zero.

These outcomes encourage players to consider the consequences of their decisions instead of simply completing tasks as quickly as possible.

The intended educational impact is to introduce younger audiences to:

  • Space science and planetary exploration.
  • Engineering systems and troubleshooting.
  • Energy and resource management.
  • Environmental protection and radiation shielding.
  • Scientific observation and sample analysis.
  • Critical thinking and problem-solving.
  • Systems thinking and decision-making under constraints.

By combining scientific explanations with interactive challenges, LOST SIGNAL aims to make STEM concepts more approachable and encourage curiosity about science, engineering and future human exploration of Mars.

8. Future Development and Vision

LOST SIGNAL is designed as a foundation that could be expanded into a broader educational space-exploration experience.

Future development opportunities include additional missions, more advanced engineering challenges, expanded planetary exploration, additional scientific experiments and new scenarios involving different environmental conditions.

The game could also introduce classroom-oriented features, additional educational assessment activities and more mission reports to help teachers connect gameplay with STEM learning objectives.

Our long-term vision is to create an accessible educational experience in which young learners do not simply read about space exploration but actively participate in the decisions, experiments and engineering challenges that make it possible.

LOST SIGNAL: 10 DAYS — Every decision matters. Every system keeps the mission alive.
